lesson.title: Speak, Hands, for Me!
lesson.subtitle: The du-command is the bare stem: Komm! Lern! Iss! — the imperative you already own

hook.title: The Command You Already Give
hook.content: Here is a secret: you have been commanding in German your whole life. When you say Speak! or Come here! or Help! — no do-support, no subject, just the bare verb — you are using the ancient Germanic imperative, word for word. German never changed the deal: Komm! Geh! Lern! The du-command is simply the stem with nothing attached — the same weapon Shakespeare's Casca grabs when he shouts 'Speak, hands, for me!' seconds before Caesar falls. English trimmed its endings away; German kept the kit, including a fossil you will recognize: Komm! can wear an optional -e (Komme!), the same final -e that once ended every English command.

footnotes.title: Speak, Hands, for Me!
footnotes.content: Julius Caesar, Act 3, Scene 1: as the conspirators close in, Casca cries 'Speak, hands, for me!' — a bare-stem imperative with no auxiliary. The line is a working demonstration that English's command form is the same construction as Komm! and Sprich!.

pattern.title: The Bare Stem — and the Vowel That Stays
pattern.content: The rule is one step: strip -en, and what is left IS the command — lernen → Lern! kommen → Komm! gehen → Geh! trinken → Trink! machen → Mach! No ending, no pronoun. Now the twist you already know from the Thou -st Circuit: verbs whose du-form changes its vowel keep the changed vowel in the command — essen: du isst → Iss! sprechen: du sprichst → Sprich! helfen: du hilfst → Hilf! The command simply borrows whatever stem the du-form uses. (geben will join this club with gib in topic 19.) One warning, honestly: verbs that only UMLAUT in the du-form (du fährst) drop the dots for the command — the command is plain Fahr! The umlaut rides with the -st, not with the stem.

footnotes.title: The Optional -e
footnotes.content: Komm! and Komme! are both correct — the -e is an older, more formal flavor that survives in songs, poetry and Luther's Bible. English once had the same choice: 'Hear me!' and 'Hear ye!' — and Old English commands ended in the very same -e.

exercises.prompt: Match each English command with its German twin:
exercises.meaning: come, go, eat, speak — as commands
exercises.explanation: The command is the bare stem: komm-, geh- — and the e→i stem-changers (Iss!, Sprich!) keep their changed vowel, exactly like their du-forms.

exercises.prompt: Command one friend to eat. Du isst — so you say:
exercises.explanation: essen's du-form is du isst (e→i) — the command keeps that vowel: Iss! The other forms belong to ihr (Esst!) and Sie (Essen Sie!).

exercises.prompt: Assemble the informal du-command with its object: 'Speak German!'
exercises.explanation: sprechen keeps its e→i vowel in the command: Sprich! — the same stem you drilled in du sprichst.

exercises.prompt: How does German structure this command word-for-word?
exercises.explanation: In a du-command, the verb stem 'Steh' takes position 1 with no 'du', while the separable prefix 'auf' still anchors the end of the frame. [Ref: Hilf]

exercises.prompt: Assemble the command chain: 'Come and drink tea'
exercises.meaning: Komm und trink Tee = come and drink tea

vocab_hints.note: bare stem of trinken — no ending, no pronoun

exercises.explanation: Two bare-stem commands chained with und — the way real German dialogue strings orders: Komm! Trink!

summary.outcome: Form du-commands as bare stems, keeping the e→i vowel of stem-changers.
summary.takeaway: The du-command is the stem: Lern! Komm! — and stem-changers keep their vowel: Iss! Sprich! Hilf!
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: Kommen Sie! Kommt! — the formal and the plural imperatives, plus the one irregular command, Sei!.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Speak, Hands, for Me! (Komm und trink Tee = come and drink tea):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Komm und trink Tee" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Speak, Hands, for Me! without relying on short-term echo.

essen.shift_rule: T → S / SS / Z + Ablaut Vowels
essen.context_translation: What do we want to eat?
essen.etymology_derivation: Medial t → ss. Noun: das Essen (food).

helfen.etymology_derivation: p → f. Governs the dative case (mir).

lernen.context_translation: I am learning German with Brücke.
lernen.etymology_derivation: Shared root *liznōną (to follow a track/learn) + infinitive -en.

trinken.context_translation: I drink a glass of water.

amerika.etymology_derivation: The same name as English America; shared proper name. [wiktionary]

geschenk.etymology_derivation: ge- + schenken (pour, serve); no English cognate — memorize this one (das Gift is the trap word). [wiktionary]

pilz.context_translation: The mushroom grows in the forest.
pilz.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic bulit, an early borrowing of Latin boletus, the porcini mushroom; English bolete is a direct loan of the same Latin word. [wiktionary]

schwierig.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German swiric 'full of boils', built on Schwäre 'ulcer'; Wiktionary warns it is often connected to schwer but is unrelated. [wiktionary]

sterben.etymology_derivation: From Old High German stërban, from Proto-Germanic *sterbaną. English starve is the sole listed English cognate, once meaning simply to die. [wiktionary]

wecker.context_phrase: Mein Wecker klingelt um sechs Uhr.
wecker.context_translation: My alarm clock rings at six o'clock.
wecker.etymology_derivation: wecken, to wake, + the agent suffix -er — literally a waker. [wiktionary]

anker.context_phrase: Das Schiff setzt den Anker aus.
anker.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *ankurô, from Latin ancora, from Greek ankura — the same Greek-Latin borrowing as English anchor. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
